stem: Stock A has σ = 25% and Stock B has σ = 15%, and the two are perfectly positively correlated (ρ = +1). What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 40% in A and 60% in B (% per annum)?

steps.label: Weighted risk of A, w_A σ_A
Weighted risk of B, w_B σ_B

solution: With ρ = 1 the formula is a perfect square: σ_P = √(w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B)² = w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

errors.label: Reported the variance (361) scaled to a decimal percent
errors.explain: 361 is the variance; the SD is its square root.

errors.label: Added the stand-alone SDs with no weights
errors.explain: Each SD is multiplied by its weight; the weights sum to 1.

explanation: ρ = +1 is the one case where risk is linear: σ_P = 0.4(25) + 0.6(15) = 19.00%. Any ρ < 1 would give less than this, which is why 19% is the upper limit for every mix of these two stocks.

stem: Stock A has σ = 30% and Stock B has σ = 20%, and the two are perfectly negatively correlated (ρ = −1). What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 60% in A and 40% in B (% per annum)?

steps.label: Weighted risk of A, w_A σ_A
Weighted risk of B, w_B σ_B

solution: With ρ = −1 the formula is the perfect square (w_Aσ_A − w_Bσ_B)², so σ_P = |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B|

errors.label: Reported the variance (as a decimal) instead of its square root
errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

errors.label: Used ρ = +1 in the cross-term (added the two risks)
errors.explain: The cross-term is 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B with ρ = −1: it subtracts 288, it does not add it.

explanation: At ρ = −1 the two risks offset: σ_P = |18% − 8%| = 10.00%, far below the 26.00% weighted average. Changing the weights to 40/60 would give 12% − 12% = 0, a riskless portfolio.

stem: Of a $40,000 portfolio, $25,000 is invested in a Canadian equity fund with σ = 19.2% and the rest in Treasury bills. What is the portfolio's standard deviation (% per annum)?
solution: T-bills have σ = 0 and ρ = 0 with the fund, so the formula reduces to σ_P = w_P σ_P

errors.label: Used the T-bill weight (0.375)
errors.explain: The risk comes from the equity fund, so its weight (0.625) multiplies σ.

errors.label: Reported the fund's own SD
errors.explain: Holding part of the money in T-bills scales the risk down in proportion.

errors.label: Squared the weight and σ without a square root (decimal variance)
errors.explain: σ_P = w σ already; no squaring is needed for the risk-free mix.

explanation: With a risk-free asset the cross-term and the risk-free variance both vanish, so σ_P is simply the risky weight times the risky σ: 0.625 × 19.2% = 12.00%. This straight-line scaling is why a capital allocation line is a straight line.

stem: You use $40,000 of your own money and borrow $20,000 at the risk-free rate of 3% per annum, investing all $60,000 in a fund with E[R] = 9% and σ = 14%. What is the standard deviation of the return on your own $40,000 (% per annum)?
solution: Weights on your own money: w_fund = 60,000/40,000 = 1.50 and w_F = −20,000/40,000 = −0.50
σ_P = w_fund × σ_fund (the risk-free asset adds no variance) = 1.50 × 14% = 21.00%

errors.label: Reported the fund's own SD
errors.explain: Borrowing to hold 150% of your capital in the fund multiplies the risk by 1.5.

errors.label: Used the borrowing weight (0.5)
errors.explain: The fund weight is 1.5, not 0.5; the risk-free weight is −0.5.

errors.label: Counted the loan as a positive 0.5 weight: (1.5 + 0.5) × 14
errors.explain: Borrowing is a negative weight; the weights must sum to 1 (1.5 − 0.5), and the risk-free asset adds no risk.

explanation: Leverage scales risk linearly: σ_P = 1.5 × 14% = 21.00%. The loan has no variance (it is risk-free), so all of the risk comes from the 150% position in the fund.

stem: You hold $30,000 of Stock A (σ = 28%) and $20,000 of Stock B (σ = 16%). The correlation between them is 0.2. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio (% per annum)?

errors.label: Reported the variance (as a decimal) instead of its square root
errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Used the weighted average of the two SDs (the ρ = 1 shortcut)
errors.explain: w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B is the answer only when ρ = 1; for ρ < 1 the portfolio SD is smaller.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

explanation: Convert dollars to weights first (0.60, 0.40), then apply σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B) = 19.14%, below the 23.20% weighted average.

stem: Invest 75% of your funds in Asset X (E[R] = 9%, σ = 14%) and 25% in Asset Y (E[R] = 15%, σ = 20%). The correlation between X and Y is 0.3. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio (% per annum)?

errors.label: Reported the variance (as a decimal) instead of its square root
errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Used the weighted average of the two SDs (the ρ = 1 shortcut)
errors.explain: w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B is the answer only when ρ = 1; for ρ < 1 the portfolio SD is smaller.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

explanation: Return is a weighted average (10.50%) but risk is not: σ_P = 12.91% is less than the weighted average of 15.5% because ρ = 0.3 < 1. Report the pair (10.50%, 12.91%) as the portfolio's point on the risk-return diagram.

stem: A portfolio is 50% Stock A and 50% Stock B. Boom (probability 0.25): A 20%, B −4%. Normal (0.50): A 8%, B 6%. Recession (0.25): A −10%, B 14%. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio's return (% per annum)?
solution: Portfolio return in each state: Boom 0.5(20) + 0.5(−4) = 8%; Normal 0.5(8) + 0.5(6) = 7%; Recession 0.5(−10) + 0.5(14) = 2%
σ_P = √5.50 = 2.35% per annum (the formula route gives the same: σ_A = 10.71%, σ_B = 6.38%, cov = −66.75 %² = −0.006675 in decimals, ρ = −0.98)

errors.label: Reported the variance (5.50) instead of its square root
errors.explain: 5.50 is a variance in %²; the SD is its square root.

errors.label: Weighted average of the two stocks' SDs (10.71% and 6.38%)
errors.explain: The two stocks are almost perfectly negatively correlated (ρ ≈ −0.98), so averaging their SDs overstates the risk by a wide margin.

errors.label: Gave the three states equal weight
errors.explain: States have probabilities 0.25/0.50/0.25; equal weighting changes both the mean and the variance.

explanation: When the data are given by state, the quickest route is to compute the portfolio's return in every state and then treat it as a single asset: E[R_P] = 6.00%, σ_P² = 5.50, σ_P = 2.35%. The formula route (σ's, cov, weights) gives the same answer; A and B hedge each other so risk falls from about 8.5% (the weighted average) to 2.35%.

stem: The correlation coefficient ρ_AB between the returns of stocks A and B is:
options: cov(A,B) / σ_B², the slope of A's returns on B's returns
cov(A,B) / (σ_A σ_B), a unit-free number between −1 and +1
cov(A,B) × σ_A × σ_B, a number in squared percent
σ_A σ_B / cov(A,B), which is always above 1
explanation: ρ_AB = cov(A,B)/(σ_A σ_B) standardizes the covariance by the two standard deviations, so it has no units and lies in [−1, +1]. Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope (beta-type measure), not a correlation.

stem: Which pair of stocks is most likely to have the highest correlation of returns?
options: Two Canadian chartered banks
A Calgary oil producer and a Vancouver software company
A Canadian bank and a Japanese automaker
A gold miner and a regulated electric utility
explanation: Stocks in the same industry and the same country respond to the same news (interest rates, regulation, the Canadian economy), so their returns move together and ρ is high and positive. Different industries or different countries have lower correlations, and lower correlation means a bigger diversification benefit.

stem: A scatter plot puts Stock A's yearly returns on the horizontal axis and Stock B's on the vertical axis. The points sit tightly around a straight line sloping downward from left to right. The correlation is closest to:
explanation: A downward-sloping tight cloud means that when A is high B is low: strong negative correlation, near −1. A formless blob is near 0, and an upward-sloping tight line is near +1.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts covariance and correlation?
options: Covariance is bounded by ±1, whereas correlation is measured in squared percent
Covariance and correlation always have opposite signs for the same pair of stocks
Correlation measures the average return of two stocks, covariance measures their risk
Correlation is covariance scaled by σ_A σ_B: unit-free and bounded by ±1, unlike covariance
explanation: Both share the same sign (the sign of the co-movement). Dividing the covariance by σ_A σ_B removes the units and caps the result at ±1 so strengths are comparable across pairs; the raw covariance grows with the stocks' volatility.

stem: Which of the following could NOT be the correlation coefficient between two stocks?
explanation: Correlation is always between −1 and +1, so +1.20 is impossible; it signals an arithmetic or units error, for example mixing percent and decimals.

stem: Why do we divide the covariance by σ_A σ_B to get the correlation?
options: It converts the covariance from percent into dollars
It makes the covariance equal to the portfolio's expected return
It removes the units, so ρ shows only the direction and strength of co-movement
It ensures that the correlation always comes out positive
explanation: A covariance of 0.03 could be strong for two calm stocks or weak for two volatile ones. Dividing by σ_A σ_B standardizes the relationship so that +1, 0 and −1 mean the same thing for every pair.

stem: A student computes cov(A,B), σ_A and σ_B from a five-year sample, but divides all three sums by N = 5 instead of N − 1 = 4. What happens to the correlation?
options: It becomes too high by a factor of 5/4
It is unchanged, because the same factor cancels
It becomes too low by a factor of 4/5
It is no longer bounded by ±1
explanation: Each of cov, σ_A² and σ_B² is a sum divided by N or N − 1. In ρ = cov/(σ_Aσ_B) the denominators are the same factor 1/(N−1) in numerator and in √(σ_A² σ_B²), so it cancels. (Mixing N for one term and N − 1 for another would, however, bias ρ.)

stem: The correlation between two Canadian bank stocks is estimated at 0.85. What does this imply for combining them in a portfolio?
options: Some benefit remains because ρ < 1, but it is small since the stocks move together
There is no diversification benefit at all, since the correlation is positive
The portfolio will be riskless, because stocks that move together offset each other
The portfolio's expected return will be lower than either stock's
explanation: Any ρ below 1 gives some benefit (σ_P lower than the weighted average of the σ's), but at 0.85 the cross-term is almost at its maximum so the gain is modest. The benefit comes at no cost in expected return because E[R_P] is a weighted average.

stem: cov(A,B) = −0.0150. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The two stocks are perfectly negatively correlated
The stocks are uncorrelated because the number is close to zero
One of the stocks must have a negative expected return
The returns tend to move in opposite directions; strength needs ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B)
explanation: The sign shows direction (negative: when A is above its mean B tends to be below its mean). The size depends on the stocks' volatilities, so −0.0150 could be anything from weak to perfect negative correlation until it is converted to ρ.

stem: A student reports a correlation of 1.18 between two stocks. What is the best interpretation?
options: The stocks are more than perfectly correlated, so diversification will increase risk
It is valid if the covariance is large enough
The value is impossible: ρ must lie in [−1, +1], so there is a units or arithmetic error to find
It indicates leveraged stocks with betas above 1
explanation: A correlation outside [−1, +1] is always a mistake: typically a wrong denominator (for example dividing by one variance, or by σ_A σ_B in different units), a unit mix of percent and decimals, or an arithmetic slip. Recheck before using the number.

stem: Every return on Stock A is doubled (a 2× leveraged version, A' = 2A) while Stock B is unchanged. What happens to cov(A',B) and to ρ(A',B) compared with cov(A,B) and ρ(A,B)?
options: Both double
The covariance doubles; the correlation is unchanged
The covariance is unchanged; the correlation doubles
Both are unchanged
explanation: cov(2A, B) = 2 cov(A,B), but σ_(2A) = 2σ_A as well, so ρ = 2cov/(2σ_A σ_B) is unchanged. This is why correlation, not covariance, describes the pattern of co-movement independent of scale.

stem: Returns of two stocks over five years are given. The sample covariance is the sum of products of deviations from the means divided by:
options: The sum of the probabilities
explanation: The professor uses the sample version (÷(N − 1)) for a short history such as five years of one stock, and the population version (÷N) only when the data are the whole population. Probabilities are used instead of a divisor when returns are given by state of the economy.

stem: Returns of two stocks are listed for three states of the economy with probabilities 0.20, 0.50 and 0.30. How is cov(A,B) computed?
options: Σ p_i (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]), with no division by N − 1
Σ (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]) / (N − 1) with N = 3
Σ p_i R_A,i R_B,i, without subtracting the means
Σ p_i (R_A,i − R_B,i)², the squared difference between the two stocks' returns
explanation: With probabilities given, each state's deviation product is weighted by its probability: cov = Σ p (R_A − E_A)(R_B − E_B). Dividing by N − 1 is for historical samples; skipping the deviations gives E[R_A R_B], which is not the covariance.

stem: If cov(A,B) = 0, then the correlation between A and B is 0.
options: True
False
explanation: True. ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B), so a zero numerator gives ρ = 0 (as long as both σ are positive). Uncorrelated stocks have no cross-term in the portfolio variance.

stem: A correlation of −0.9 between two stocks indicates a stronger linear relationship than a correlation of +0.3.
options: True
False
explanation: True. Strength is the magnitude |ρ| (0.9 versus 0.3); the sign only gives the direction. −0.9 means the stocks move almost exactly opposite to each other, the best case for diversification.

stem: A correlation of 0.5 between A and B means that B's return is always exactly half of A's return.
options: True
False
explanation: False. A correlation of 0.5 describes a loose tendency to move together; it says nothing about a fixed proportion. Only |ρ| = 1 means an exact linear relationship.

stem: Two stocks in the same industry and the same country tend to have a _____ correlation.
options: low positive
negative
high positive
zero
explanation: Common industry and country factors drive both stocks, so their returns rise and fall together; stocks in different industries or countries have lower correlations and offer more diversification.

stem: Stock A has σ = 24% and Stock B has σ = 15%; cov(A,B) = 0.0180 (decimals). What is the correlation between A and B?
explanation: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B) = 0.0180/(0.24 × 0.15) = 0.0180/0.0360 = 0.50. Dividing by σ_A² (0.31) or σ_B² (0.80) gives a beta-type slope, and reporting 0.02 simply quotes the covariance as if it were ρ.

stem: In three equally likely states of the economy, Stock X returns 15%, 6% and −3%, and Stock Y returns 4%, 10% and 10%. What is cov(X,Y), with returns as decimals?
explanation: E[R_X] = 6%, E[R_Y] = 8%. Deviation products (decimals): 0.09 × (−0.04) = −0.0036, 0 × 0.02 = 0, (−0.09)(0.02) = −0.0018. With probability 1/3 each, cov = (−0.0036 + 0 − 0.0018)/3 = −0.0018. Dividing by N − 1 gives −0.0027, leaving the sum undivided gives −0.0054, and skipping the means (E[XY]) gives 0.0030.

stem: Stock A has σ = 18% and Stock B has σ = 30%; their correlation is −0.5. What is cov(A,B), with returns as decimals?
explanation: cov(A,B) = ρ σ_A σ_B = (−0.5)(0.18)(0.30) = −0.0270. The positive 0.0270 loses the sign, −0.0900 omits σ_B, and −0.1200 uses the average of the two σ's in place of their product.

stem: Strong economy (probability 0.30): Stock A returns 18%, Stock B 6%. Moderate (0.50): A 9%, B 8%. Weak (0.20): A −6%, B 20%. What is the correlation between A and B?
keystrokes: Use the statistics (2nd DATA) or compute by hand: 0.3 × 9.3 × (−3.8) = −10.602

errors.label: Summed the deviation products without weighting by the probabilities
errors.explain: Each state's deviation product must be multiplied by its probability; an unweighted sum treats the states as equally likely.

errors.label: Reported the covariance (in decimals) as the correlation
errors.explain: The covariance still carries the units of σ_A σ_B; divide by σ_A σ_B to get ρ.

errors.label: Divided the covariance in %² by σ's in decimals
errors.explain: Mixing percent and decimal units gives a nonsense ρ far outside [−1, 1].

explanation: ρ_AB = −0.95: the two stocks move almost exactly opposite across the three states, so a portfolio of both would remove most of the risk. Always compute E first, then deviations, then probability-weighted squares and products; a ρ outside [−1, 1] means a units slip.

stem: In three equally likely states, Stock A returns 14%, 6% and −2%, while Stock B returns 3%, 7% and 11%. What is the correlation between A and B?
solution: ρ = −21.33/(6.532 × 3.266) = −1.00: B is an exact decreasing straight-line function of A (B falls 0.5 for every 1 that A rises)

errors.label: Reported the covariance (in decimals) as the correlation
errors.explain: A covariance of −0.0021 is not a correlation; divide by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only (the slope of B on A)
errors.explain: Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope (−0.50), not the correlation, which divides by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Used Σ p R_A R_B instead of deviation products
errors.explain: Covariance is built from deviations from the means; E[R_A R_B] alone is not the covariance.

explanation: ρ = −1.00 exactly: B is a perfect decreasing straight-line function of A. A perfectly negatively correlated pair is the strongest diversifier: the right weights make σ_P zero.

stem: Over five years, Stock A returned 12%, −4%, 18%, 6% and 8%, and Stock B returned 5%, 9%, 1%, 7% and 3% (same years, same order). Using sample statistics (divide by N − 1), what is the correlation between A and B?
solution: Sum of products = 0 − 48 − 40 − 4 + 0 = −92, so cov = −92/4 = −23 %² = −0.0023 in decimals
keystrokes: 2nd DATA, enter X and Y pairs, 2nd STAT (LIN mode): Sx = 8.124, Sy = 3.162, r = −0.895

errors.label: Divided the covariance by N = 5 but the standard deviations by N − 1 = 4
errors.explain: All three quantities must use the same divisor; mixing N and N − 1 distorts ρ (here it shrinks it).

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only (the slope of B on A)
errors.explain: Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope, not the correlation.

errors.label: Reported the covariance in decimals as the correlation
errors.explain: −0.0023 is a covariance; ρ needs the division by σ_A σ_B.

explanation: With sample data use N − 1 throughout (and the same factor for cov, σ_A and σ_B): ρ ≈ −0.90. A strongly negative correlation means these two stocks are excellent diversifiers.

stem: Over five years, Stock X returned 8%, 2%, 14%, 6% and 10%, and Stock Y returned 9%, 3%, 12%, 6% and 5% (same years, same order). Compute the sample covariance of their returns, entering returns as decimals (for example 8% = 0.08).

errors.label: Divided by N = 5 instead of N − 1 = 4
errors.explain: Five years of one stock's history is a sample: divide by N − 1.

errors.label: Worked in percent units: 52 %² ÷ 4
errors.explain: The question asks for decimals; 13 %² equals 0.0013 in decimal form.

errors.label: Did not divide the sum of products
errors.explain: A covariance is an average of the deviation products, so divide by N − 1.

explanation: The sample covariance is Σ(R_X − mean)(R_Y − mean)/(N − 1) = 0.0052/4 = 0.0013 in decimals (13 in %² units). It is positive because the two stocks tended to be above or below their averages in the same years.

stem: Stock A has σ = 20% and Stock B has σ = 25%, and the correlation between them is 0.4. What is the covariance of their returns, as a decimal?

errors.label: Multiplied the percentages directly (20 × 25 × 0.4)
errors.explain: σ must be written as decimals (0.20, 0.25); 200 is the covariance in %² units.

errors.label: Divided ρ by σ_A σ_B
errors.explain: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B), so cov = ρ σ_A σ_B, not ρ ÷ (σ_A σ_B).

errors.label: Forgot one σ: ρ × σ_A
errors.explain: The covariance needs both standard deviations.

explanation: cov(A,B) = ρ σ_A σ_B = 0.0200. This is the quantity you can drop straight into the covariance form of the portfolio variance: 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B).

stem: Stock A has σ = 14% and Stock B has σ = 10%; cov(A,B) = 0.0105 (decimals). What is the correlation between A and B?

errors.label: Reported the covariance as the correlation
errors.explain: The covariance is not bounded by ±1 and keeps squared-return units; divide by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only
errors.explain: That is the slope of B on A (a beta-type number), not the correlation.

errors.label: Divided a decimal covariance by the σ product in percent (14 × 10)
errors.explain: Use decimals for both cov and σ (or percent for both).

explanation: ρ = 0.0105/(0.14 × 0.10) = 0.75: a strong positive correlation, so the pair offers only a modest diversification benefit.

stem: Stock A has σ = 16%. The covariance of A and B is 0.0156 (decimals) and their correlation is 0.65. What is Stock B's standard deviation (% per annum)?
solution: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B) rearranges to σ_A σ_B = cov/ρ = 0.0156/0.65 = 0.0240

errors.label: Ignored the correlation: cov ÷ σ_A
errors.explain: cov = ρ σ_A σ_B, so ρ must be divided out as well.

errors.label: Multiplied by ρ instead of dividing
errors.explain: ρ = cov/(σ_Aσ_B), so σ_B = cov/(ρ σ_A); ρ belongs in the denominator.

errors.label: Divided by ρ σ_A² (variance of A)
errors.explain: σ_A σ_B is a product of two standard deviations; only one is known, so divide by the known σ_A (not its square).

stem: The diversification benefit of combining two stocks is best described as:
options: the amount by which σ_P falls below the weighted average of the stocks' σ's, available whenever ρ < 1
the higher expected return earned by holding two stocks instead of one
the complete elimination of risk once at least ten stocks are held
the risk reduction that occurs only when the stocks are negatively correlated
explanation: The benefit is the gap between w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B (the ρ = 1 risk) and the actual σ_P. It exists for every ρ below 1, not only negative ones, it costs no expected return, and it never removes systematic risk.

stem: A 50/50 mix of two stocks with σ = 15% and σ = 19% has a portfolio standard deviation of 13.1%. The gap between 13.1% and the weighted average of 17.0% is an illustration of:
options: a risk premium
domination
the diversification benefit
systematic risk
explanation: The weighted average (17.0%) is what the portfolio would have if the stocks were perfectly correlated; the actual 13.1% is lower because ρ < 1. That shortfall is the diversification benefit.

stem: On a risk-return diagram (σ on the horizontal axis, E[R] on the vertical axis), the curve traced by all mixes of two stocks bows to the left of the straight line joining them. What does this tell you about ρ_AB?
options: ρ_AB = 1: there is no diversification benefit
ρ_AB > 1: the portfolios are riskier than the stocks themselves
Nothing: the curve's shape depends only on the expected returns
ρ_AB < 1: the mixes are less risky than the weighted average of the two risks
explanation: The straight line is the ρ = 1 case (σ_P is the weighted average of the σ's). Any curve bowed to the left means σ_P is below that line for the same expected return, so ρ < 1. The lower the correlation, the stronger the bow.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the set of two-stock portfolios on a risk-return diagram (σ on the horizontal axis)?
options: ρ = 1: a curve bowed to the left; ρ = 0: a straight line; ρ = −1: a straight line
ρ = 1: a straight line; ρ = 0: a curve bowed to the left; ρ = −1: two straight segments touching σ_P = 0
ρ = 1: two straight segments touching σ_P = 0; ρ = 0: a straight line; ρ = −1: a straight line
The shape is the same for every ρ; only the length of the curve changes
explanation: At ρ = 1 risk is linear in the weights, so the mixes lie on a straight line. At ρ = 0 the curve bows to the left. At ρ = −1 the σ_P formula is a perfect square |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B|, giving two straight segments that touch σ_P = 0 at the hedging weights.

stem: In which of the following cases is there NO diversification benefit from mixing two stocks?
options: ρ_AB = 0
ρ_AB = +1
explanation: A benefit exists whenever ρ < 1; it is just small when ρ is close to 1 (such as 0.95). Only perfect positive correlation makes σ_P exactly equal to the weighted average of the σ's.

stem: Why does diversification reduce risk without reducing expected return?
options: Because diversified portfolios are always invested in the stock with the highest expected return
Because a lower correlation between the stocks raises the portfolio's expected return
Because E[R_P] is just a weighted average, while σ_P falls when the stocks do not move in lockstep
Because risk and return are unrelated for portfolios
explanation: Return is linear in the weights (no correlation term) while risk is not. Lower correlation lowers σ_P but leaves E[R_P] untouched, so diversification is called the only 'free lunch' in finance (risk falls with no loss of expected return).
